Open operating framework · community edition

Your data already exists. What's missing is who answers for it.

Numbers that don't match across departments, nobody knows who approves access, the audit asks for proof and there are only emails. KDV turns data governance into routine: every shared dataset gets an accountable owner, an agreement of use, rule-based access and evidence of the value it creates.

What KDV does

Data governance as everyday work, not a separate project.

Start with a single use case. Every delivery records who decided, what was agreed and what value it created.

01 · Owner

Someone answers for every shared dataset.

An owner and a steward named for each business domain and data product.

02 · Agreement and rule-based access

One agreed definition and time-limited access.

A versioned contract states what the data means and what it may be used for; the platform enforces the access policy.

03 · Evidence

Proof produced by the work itself.

Decisions, tests and usage leave evidence for review. They support assessment and improvement without producing an automatic maturity score.

How it works

Four stages, from raw data to observed value.

Choose a stage to see what to do, who takes part and what evidence is kept. Before them, a short preparation scopes the first case.

Starts when

A defined use case and an identified source.

What to do

  • Connect the sources
  • Document the origin
  • Prepare the data
  • Establish a reproducible delivery

Evidence kept

  • Source inventory
  • Record of transformations (lineage)
  • Initial quality tests

The minimum every shared dataset needs

Five common items. Everything else, each organisation decides.

Role names, approval flows and review rhythm can be adapted. These five items cannot be removed.

01Named ownerWithout an owner, nobody answers for errors, changes or access requests.02Versioned contractNumbers diverge when each area uses its own definition.03ClassificationThe rule of use depends on how sensitive the data is.04Policy-based accessAccess granted by email is rarely revoked.05AuditabilityAudits and data protection law ask for proof, not intent.

Why a hive?

We use your terms first. The hive only helps you remember.

Hives cooperate without central command: each looks after its own and respects common rules. It is an organisational metaphor; it does not replace your organisation's terms or assign roles based on bee biology.

Select a row to see the concept without leaving this page.

What your organisation calls itKDV termExample
Ecosystem
The boundary of collaboration: who takes part, for what purpose and under which common rules.		EcosystemA network of regional councils sharing professional registration data; a business group with several companies; a municipality whose departments exchange indicators.
Business domain
The business area accountable for the meaning and priorities of a set of data.		HiveFinance; Customer service; Professional registration; Inspection.
Business subdomain
The sub-area, team or process where data is prepared and from which products come.		CellAccounts payable (in Finance); Enforcement notices (in Inspection).
Business grouping
An optional grouping of subdomains within the same domain, for shared rules or permissions.		Comb“Revenue”, bringing together Billing and Invoicing within Finance.
Data product
A trustworthy set of data, published with an owner, a contract and known consumers.		Data productWeekly order aggregate; professional register API; inspection prioritisation dashboard.
Execution environment
Where products are prepared and operated: production, staging, development.		FarmProduction; Staging; Development.

Illustrative examples

Different contexts. The same questions.

Who is accountable? What was agreed? Who may use it? What value did it create?

From conflicting sales reports to an agreed revenue product.

Finance and Sales agree definitions, refresh, an owner and a versioned contract. The board discusses the decision, not the number.

See across the four stagesRead the full example
  1. CultivateInventory of invoicing and CRM sources
  2. GovernA single definition of “recognised revenue” in the contract
  3. SharePolicy-based access for commercial teams
  4. ActivateIndicator: meetings without manual reconciliation of numbers

Anticipate pressure on services with data from scattered systems.

Permitted indicators from different departments and sector systems are combined, with clear refresh, coverage and limits, to support proactive management.

See across the four stagesRead the full example
  1. CultivateInventory of each department's sources
  2. GovernAgreement on geography, period and suppression of small groups
  3. ShareAggregated product, without identifiable records
  4. ActivateIndicator: demand by area before the planning meeting

Prioritise inspections with current, traceable information.

Authorised internal and external sources are matched. Analytical prioritisation is kept separate from the evidence and human decision required in each individual case.

See across the four stagesRead the full example
  1. CultivateInventory of registrations, complaints and public sources
  2. GovernVersioned matching rules and human review
  3. SharePlanning product and restricted per-case view
  4. ActivateIndicator: inspections that confirm an irregularity

Fictitious scenarios. They are not customer cases or delivery commitments.
